title: The Student-by-Student Ground Game for Teacher Credibility
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart offers a systematic way for teachers to build credibility quickly, modeled on Kevin Hart's fan-by-fan touring strategy described in Ryan Holiday's Perennial Seller. The teacher aims to create a moment of genuine connection with every student at least once, tracks it with a deliberately simple system, then repeats and expands to other students, staff and parents. He gives guardrails against seeming inauthentic: don't take notes mid-conversation, keep interactions short, treat it as a skill that improves with practice, and expect the payoff to come slowly through word of mouth. The central claim is that credibility is earned person by person through many small, quick moments of care, not through one grand gesture.
points: Credibility can be built deliberately by collecting many quick moments of genuine connection with individual students.
The tracking system must be very simple, such as one sheet of names or a composition notebook, or it will not survive.
Tracking must be invisible to the student, and brief hallway or independent-work conversations beat rare long ones.
The payoff is slow word-of-mouth reputation, and it still requires energy and wisdom in every lesson.
quotes: So listen: we don’t have assistants, and there’s no national travel included in our job. But we can take some clear things away in creating our own, scaled-down “student-by-student” ground game.
Step 1: Start with the kids on your roster. Your objective is going to be to create a moment of genuine connection with every kid at least once.
Step 2: Devise a simple (!!!) system for keeping track. Listen, you’ve got a complex job, you don’t need another complex thing to operate. This ground game needs to be simple.
1) Don’t keep track of the conversation while it’s happening. Put the clipboard somewhere else. People don’t like to feel like projects or data points.

I try to make MGCs during passing times between classes, when I chance upon kids in the hallways during my prep, and during independent work segments of my lessons using hallway pull-outs. But they’re quick. I’m going for a large quantity of nice, even powerful moments, not a small quantity of long and deep conversations.
4) Keep your eye on the long game. When we do this, it’s not going to magically fix our credibility issues. But when we do it for months, we’re going to learn a ton about the cultures of our kids.
You’ll still have to work for it with each new person you meet and with those kids you already know. You’ll still need to bring the ruckus, the energy, the passion, the wisdom to every lesson.
